kernelIdea: Proving ¬q ⇒ ¬p proves p ⇒ q. Choose it when the hypothesis you are handed is awkward to compute with.

kernels.l1: Sometimes the easy way to check a promise is to check it backwards.
kernels.l2: You can show a promise is kept by flipping it around the good way first, and then showing the flipped one is kept.
kernels.l3: Because a claim and its contrapositive are always worth the same, you may prove the contrapositive instead. Do that when the if part you were handed is hard to work with.
kernels.l4: Because a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, proving one proves the other. Choose the contrapositive when the hypothesis you were handed is negative or awkward.
kernels.l5: Proof by contrapositive replaces the goal with its contrapositive, which says the same thing. Choose it when the denial of the conclusion is more usable than the hypothesis you were handed.
kernels.l6: A proof by contrapositive announces the switch, proves the contrapositive directly, and invokes the equivalence to conclude the original.
kernels.l7: Proof by contrapositive proves a conditional by proving its contrapositive instead. Reach for it when the hypothesis you were handed is a denial, or when the negated conclusion breaks a compound quantity apart.
kernels.l8: Proving the contrapositive proves the original, because the two are the same statement. It differs from proof by contradiction in assuming only the denied conclusion, never the hypothesis alongside it.
